about.title: Lakewood Car Accident Claims
about.longDescription: Lakewood is a city of 81,611 people spread across a grid of wide boulevards, and most of its traffic funnels onto a handful of them. Public collision records for 2025 show 308 injury crashes here, with 441 people hurt and one death. Del Amo Boulevard, South Street, Woodruff Avenue and Carson Street account for the highest counts, and Friday evenings between 5 and 7 p.m. tend to be when reports cluster. If one of those crashes was yours, the days after can feel like a second collision: calls from adjusters, paperwork, and a body that hurts in new places. LawProactive exists to take one task off your plate. We are not a law firm. We are a free service that connects Lakewood residents with an independent personal injury attorney who handles car accident claims in Los Angeles County. The attorney reviews your situation, explains how California's pure comparative fault rule and two-year filing deadline apply, and works on contingency, so there is no fee unless your case recovers money.

whyChoose.title: Why Lakewood Drivers Turn to LawProactive

items.title: The clock is shorter than most people think
items.desc: California gives you two years to file a car accident lawsuit, but if a city or county vehicle or a road defect is involved, a government claim may be due in as little as six months. An attorney can pin down which deadline applies to your Lakewood crash before it slips by.

items.title: Partial fault does not close the door
items.desc: Under California's pure comparative fault rule, you can still recover even if you share some blame for a collision on Woodruff Avenue or South Street; your recovery is reduced by your percentage of fault rather than eliminated. That is worth knowing before an adjuster tries to talk you out of a claim.

items.title: No fee unless there is a recovery
items.desc: Every attorney in our network works on contingency, so you pay nothing up front and nothing at all if the case does not recover money. Our connection service is free, too.

items.question: The other driver's insurer wants a recorded statement about my crash on Del Amo Boulevard. Should I give one?
items.answer: You are not required to give the other driver's insurance company a recorded statement, and it is generally wise to decline until you have spoken with an attorney. Adjusters are trained to ask questions that can later be used to shift fault onto you under California's comparative fault rule. Keep your own notes, photos and the police report number, and let a lawyer handle the conversation.

items.question: What evidence should I hold on to after a Lakewood car accident?
items.answer: Save everything you can: photos of the vehicles and the intersection, the other driver's insurance card, contact details for witnesses, and the report from the Los Angeles County Sheriff's Department or CHP if one was taken. Keep medical records and receipts as they come in. Businesses along corridors like Carson Street may have camera footage that gets overwritten quickly, so an attorney will often move fast to request it.

items.question: Is there a limit on what I can recover for pain and suffering in California?
items.answer: For an ordinary car accident claim, California does not cap non-economic damages such as pain, suffering and loss of enjoyment of life. The amount depends on the specific injuries, treatment and how the crash has changed your daily routine. An attorney can walk you through what is realistic in your situation rather than guessing from averages.
